data.title: ETF Store President Nate Geraci Says CLARITY Act Faces Delay Over Crypto's Impact on Banks
data.description: ETF Store President Nate Geraci said on X that the main reason the CLARITY Act has not passed is that crypto is challenging traditional banks' business model. According to Odaily, he said the debate includes ethics provisions and BRCA-related disputes, but the core issue is that crypto is reducing the need for banks as financial intermediaries and undermining the net interest income model that supports them, along with the political forces behind it.

According to ChainCatcher, the move reflects a sudden swing in the prediction market and may be affected by breaking news.

data.title: China's Electronic Yarn and Cloth Prices Rise as AI Demand Lifts PCB Consumption
data.description: Latest data from Zhuochuang Information showed that prices for mainstream domestic electronic yarn products G75 and 7628 electronic cloth have risen sharply, with many manufacturers further increasing prices for some high-end electronic yarn models. He Li, general manager of Beijing Zhizhiyizhi'an Investment Management Co., said the price increases are mainly driven by AI-related demand upgrades, while effective supply expansion has lagged behind. He said high-end AI server PCBs use about three to five times as much electronic cloth per unit as traditional servers, and manufacturers are also shifting equipment and capital toward higher-value products such as thin cloth and low-dielectric cloth, squeezing supply of standard electronic cloth. According to Jiemian News, the tight market for electronic cloth is likely to persist in the near term.

data.title: XRPL Upgrade Proposal Would Let Banks Cover XRP Fees for Customers
data.description: A proposed XRPL upgrade could allow banks and fintech firms to pay XRP-related costs for customers who do not hold the token. According to NS3.AI, the Sponsor amendment would let companies cover account reserves and transaction fees while customers keep control of their accounts and private keys. XRPScan showed six validators supporting the amendment, which is still below the 29-validator threshold.

data.title: US MARKET CLOSE | Major Indexes Fall as AI IPO Fears and Rising Oil Prices Weigh; Nvidia Drops Over 3%
data.description: US stocks closed lower on Monday as concerns over AI safety spurred major uncertainty in the AI IPO space, compounded by the latest moves in oil prices, according to Sina Finance. The Dow fell 0.29%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.48%, and the Nasdaq declined 0.56%. Among the "Magnificent Seven," Meta Platforms rose 2.71%, Google gained 3.06%, Microsoft added 1.97%, and Apple edged up 0.24%, while Tesla fell 1.77%, Amazon lost 1.26%, and Nvidia dropped 3.36%. The most immediate risk for the market is that the billions of dollars in spending underpinning the AI boom could slow, a concern that intensified after OpenAI's Altman said the company would not pursue an initial public offering this year due to safety concerns. Kathleen Brooks, head of research at XTB, called it a very rare unified signal from a group of tech CEOs that was weighing on AI trades in early trading, and questioned whether the warnings meant hyperscale AI compute and infrastructure buildout was nearing an end. Chris Armstrong of Berenberg said irrational exuberance seen in midsummer was being squeezed out, marking a further stage of lowered market expectations. Elsewhere, Saudi Arabia shut a key pipeline that can bypass the Strait of Hormuz, pushing oil prices higher; US WTI crude futures rose 4% to break above $104 a barrel, and Brent crude gained 4% to top $109. US crude prices had broken past the $100 mark last week amid escalating Middle East conflict. The Federal Reserve will hold its September monetary policy meeting this week. According to the CME FedWatch tool, federal funds futures traders priced the probability of a Fed rate hike at about 88%, and following higher-than-expected US consumer inflation data released last Friday, traders now see the odds of a Wednesday hike at close to 90%, which would be the Fed's first hike since mid-2023. The European Central Bank raised rates last week and signaled possible further hikes if inflation continues to climb. Government bond yields edged higher, with the global bond market posting its worst week since mid-May. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield is approaching 5%, set to reach its highest since 2023, while the German 10-year yield broke above 3.53%, its highest since 2009. European indexes closed mixed, with the Stoxx 600 down 0.48%, the UK FTSE 100 up 0.4%, Germany's DAX down 0.6%, and France's CAC 40 down 0.78%. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.81%, South Korea's Kospi tumbled 3.26%, Australia's S&P 200 rose 0.10%, and mainland China's CSI 300 closed down 0.67% at 4480.08.

data.title: Thune Signals Congress May Move On AI Guardrails
data.description: According to Axios, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Congress has a role in AI oversight and that “guardrails” make sense for frontier models, while also backing a “light touch” approach that would not stifle innovation. Thune said he sees “potential consequential risks” from AI but added that people often create worst-case scenarios, and he left open the possibility of Senate action on a House bill aimed at ensuring communities do not pay more for data centers’ power use. He said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would require companies building frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight, and said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz to reintroduce it “hopefully soon.” House GOP leaders have not indicated they plan to keep the chamber in session after this week for AI legislation, while Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress may need to act but that corporate responsibility is also important.

data.title: Bonk Guy Says PONS Fundamentals Improved as Daily Revenue Tops $1 Million
data.description:
Bonk Guy said PONS fundamentals have improved during the recent consolidation period, with daily revenue staying above $1 million over the past two weeks even as interest in Robinhood Chain eased. According to Odaily, he said 80% of protocol revenue continues to be used to buy back and burn PONS, and more than 30% of the token supply has already been permanently destroyed.

He added that Pons now holds about 75% to 80% of the Robinhood Chain Launchpad market. Based on current data, annualized fees and revenue are about $829 million and $159 million, respectively, while PONS has a market capitalization of about $430 million. By comparison, PUMP has annualized fees and revenue of about $1.115 billion and $460 million, with a market capitalization of about $1.75 billion.

Bonk Guy said PONS has at least a chance to reach a circulating market capitalization of $5 billion in this cycle, more than 10 times its current level.

data.title: STOCKS | Oracle Begins Another Round of Layoffs Amid Expanded AI Spending
data.description:
Oracle has reportedly started another round of layoffs. According to Sina Finance, citing foreign media, the layoffs formally began on Monday, and an internal document showed that some teams faced cuts of double-digit percentages.

The report said a copy of the layoff notice email stated that, after careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, the company decided to eliminate the recipient's position as part of a broader organizational restructuring, making that day the employee's last day at the company.

The layoffs follow earlier cuts this year. Oracle first disclosed a restructuring plan at the start of the year, when total costs were expected to reach $2.1 billion. By April 2026, the company had begun layoffs.

In June, when Oracle released its annual report, it disclosed that headcount had fallen by 21,000 in fiscal 2026 ended May 31, 2026, a decline of 13%. Those cuts resulted in $1.84 billion in severance and termination costs. Before the latest layoffs, Oracle had about 141,000 employees.

Oracle's September quarterly report showed that management had decided to add about $700 million to the restructuring plan to reflect additional actions expected as the company pushes ahead with a costly AI data center buildout. The plan, approved in fiscal 2026, covers severance, contract termination fees, and related exit costs, indicating the layoffs are expected to expand. Oracle said part of the reason was the adoption of AI technology in some functions.

Against that backdrop, co-founder and Executive Chairman Larry Ellison canceled a plan to sell up to 50 million Oracle shares. Based on last Friday's closing price, the shares were worth about $7.5 billion. Oracle said on Saturday that no shares were sold under the plan and that Ellison had no other plans to sell Oracle stock. The company did not say why the plan was canceled.

Oracle has been investing heavily in AI data center infrastructure, betting that AI demand will keep growing. The company reported capital expenditures of $28.5 billion in fiscal 2027's first quarter, far above $8.5 billion a year earlier. It also plans to raise about $40 billion through borrowing and share issuance this fiscal year. In fiscal 2026, capital expenditures reached $55.7 billion, leaving cash outflows $23.7 billion above revenue. Oracle's total debt has reached $125 billion.

Despite the financial pressure, Oracle's first-quarter results were still strong. On September 10, Oracle reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings, with quarterly revenue up 30% year over year to $19.3 billion. Under U.S. GAAP, net income rose 60% to $4.7 billion, and earnings per share increased 55% to $1.56. Non-GAAP earnings per share were $1.92, up 30%.

Although the latest earnings report showed some positive signs, including growth in the cloud business, investor concerns about the cost of Oracle's AI expansion and questions about the future of its legacy software business have still left the stock down about 25% this year. As of the U.S. market close on September 14, Oracle shares were at $144.72, down 3.7%.

data.title: 0x Says Malicious Uniswap v4 Hooks Are Increasing
data.description:
0x said it routed 81.92 million transactions and $42.67 billion in volume this year, with about 70% touching Uniswap liquidity. According to ChainCatcher, the company said malicious Uniswap v4 hooks have recently increased, using one price in quote requests and another at settlement to profit by deceiving aggregators, wallets, and trading apps.

After analyzing 84,163 hooks across six blockchains, 0x said only 19.4% were safe, while 54.2% were malicious and 26.4% were potentially malicious. It added that transactions routed through malicious v4 hooks can end up delivering as much as 50% less than the quoted amount at execution.

0x cited examples including Base chain ETH/NVDAc pool hooks that have collected about $143,000 in fees and BNB Chain USDT/WBNB pool hooks that have collected about $18,600. The company said routers must ensure quoted amounts match actual execution behavior, applications need controls to quickly exclude suspicious routes, and users should understand that the best quote is only useful when the route is safe. 0x said it has taken measures including detection and pool reviews to keep such pools out of routing.

data.title: UK Could Add £15 Billion in Oil, Gas Tax Revenue by Advancing New Regime
data.description: The UK could raise an additional £15 billion ($20 billion) in tax revenue from oil and gas production over the next decade if Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government brings forward its new fiscal regime to next year, according to Bloomberg reported. The estimate came from an industry lobby group.

data.title: US Judge Blocks Trump Rule Limiting Foreign Students’ and Journalists’ Stay
data.description:
A federal judge in the United States on Monday suspended enforcement of a new Trump administration rule that would limit how long foreign students, journalists, and other nonimmigrant visa holders can stay in the country without a visa extension. According to Sina Finance, Boston federal district judge F. Dennis Saylor issued the ruling one day before the administration had planned to put the rule into effect.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced the rule in July as part of the Trump administration's broader effort to tighten immigration controls, saying it was aimed at what it called visa abuse by foreign students, exchange visitors, and media representatives. Under the rule, the maximum stay for holders of F nonimmigrant student visas and J exchange visitor visas would be capped at four years, while most foreign journalists would initially be limited to 240 days and could apply for one extension of up to 240 days.

data.title: Samsung Backs Dutch AI Chipmaker Euclyd in $231 Million Funding Round
data.description: According to CNBC, Samsung backed Dutch AI chipmaker Euclyd in a $231 million funding round as investment in alternatives to Nvidia's GPUs accelerates. Euclyd CEO Bernardo Kastrup said the company's 200-million-euro Series A was co-led by Somerset Capital Partners, the Scaleup Europe Fund managed by EQT, and Innovation Industries, alongside Samsung. Founded in 2024, Euclyd is developing an AI chip system for inference with a different architecture from GPUs, including processor and memory architecture. Kastrup said the company aims to reduce the energy needs and costs of AI data center infrastructure and is targeting two revenue streams: hardware and physical rack systems for enterprise customers seeking secure self-hosted AI inference, and intellectual property sales to companies building their own chips. He said Samsung can contribute engineering, supply-chain and memory expertise in addition to capital. Euclyd aims to begin rolling out its physical chip systems in 2028 and to serve thousands of enterprise customers by 2030.

data.title: Saudi-Led Coalition Says Houthi Attacks Injured 13 Civilians in Saudi Arabia
data.description: The Saudi-led coalition said Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched ballistic missiles and drone attacks on civilian targets in Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Taif on Monday, injuring 13 civilians. According to Sina Finance, coalition spokesman Major General Turki Al-Maliki said the injuries ranged from minor to serious, and that seven houses and two vehicles were damaged. He said the coalition would respond in a "responsible and decisive" manner and take what it called necessary military measures to deter further attacks.

data.title: U.S. Government Watchdog Says War Caused Strategic Stock Shortages
data.description: According to Wallstreetcn, a U.S. government watchdog on September 14 released its first report on the impact of the U.S.-Iran war, acknowledging shortages in advanced U.S. weapons stockpiles and disclosing damage to U.S. military aircraft, military bases, and diplomatic facilities in the Middle East. The Pentagon inspector general's report said the war caused "strategic stock shortages" and exposed industrial capacity bottlenecks in ammunition replenishment, while experts had previously estimated it could take about three years for the U.S. military to restore advanced missile and air-defense interceptor inventories to prewar levels.

data.title: STOCKS | Trump Energy Official Says Export Ban Would Not Lower U.S. Fuel Prices
data.description:
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said a ban on fuel or crude exports would not reduce retail oil prices. According to Sina Finance, Burgum made the remarks on Monday on the sidelines of the G20 energy summit in Houston.

Retail diesel prices have hit a record above $6 per gallon, while gasoline prices have topped $4 per gallon, prompting speculation that the Trump administration could consider export restrictions ahead of key midterm elections. Industry analysts and market observers remain divided on whether such restrictions could ease pressure on consumers over the long term.

Burgum said the administration would consider an export ban only if it believed such a move could lower prices, adding that this was not the case. He and Energy Secretary Chris Wright have publicly opposed such restrictions.

data.title: Federal Judge Orders EPA to Reverse Reclassification of California Clean Air Act Waivers
data.description: According to Wallstreetcn, a U.S. federal judge ruled that the Environmental Protection Agency must withdraw its decision to reclassify two Clean Air Act waivers granted to California as "rules" rather than "orders," and must "withdraw or correct" the move in all public statements while preventing the reclassification from taking effect. Congress is moving ahead with votes to use the Congressional Review Act to overturn the waivers, and the House plans to vote on two resolutions introduced in August on Tuesday and Thursday.
